title: Fluency Practice (with monitoring)
subtitle: The volume of practice fluency requires — delivered so the teacher sees the thinking and responds, never a silent score.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Bay-Williams & SanGiovanni, Figuring Out Fluency (2021) · NCTM (procedural fluency from conceptual understanding) · Rohrer & Bjork (interleaving) · Boaler (timed math & anxiety).

blocks.text: Repeated practice that builds **flexible, accurate, efficient** fluency — with **every student showing their work** while the teacher circulates, watches where reasoning breaks, and responds in the moment.

Fluency genuinely needs reps; the opener routines build strategies and understanding, but students also need volume to make them automatic. The key is the *wrapper*: practice with visible work and live monitoring teaches; a silent, auto-graded “7 out of 10” does not — it tells you who was wrong but never *why*.

blocks.title: The tool isn’t the problem — the wrapper is

blocks.text: A quiz app (Quizizz, 99math, etc.) is fine as a *delivery mechanism* when it’s wrapped in monitoring: students show work on paper, you circulate and catch misconceptions (“we need a common denominator because…”), and you debrief. What we move away from is the silent black-box score that hides thinking and leans on speed. Same problems, completely different learning.

blocks.text: What real fluency means (it’s not speed)

Procedural fluency is **flexibility** (choosing an efficient strategy), **accuracy**, and **efficiency** — *and* knowing which strategy fits. Practice that only rewards fast recall of one method builds none of the flexibility. So we practice with **strategy showing** and **interleaved** problem types, not one type drilled in a block.
What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Every student showing work, not just answers
The teacher circulating, catching misconceptions live
“Show your strategy” — flexibility valued, not just speed
Interleaved problem types (choose the method)
A short debrief: “what tripped people up?”

no.title: We should *not* see
items: A silent, auto-graded score with no work shown
Speed races / leaderboards as the main event
The teacher at the desk while students click
20 of the identical problem type in a block
“7/10” with no idea why the 3 were missed

blocks.title: Speed is a by-product, never the goal

blocks.text: Timed, competitive speed practice can build math anxiety and rewards the one method a student already has — it does not build flexibility, and it can dent the very disposition we’re growing. Fluency gets faster *because* it got more flexible and understood, not the other way around.

items: **Showing work lets you respond to a specific student’s misconception** in the moment — the access support a score can’t give.
**Drop the speed pressure;** turn off timers/leaderboards so slower-but-thoughtful students aren’t told daily that they’re “bad at math.”
**Interleaving** teaches all students to *choose* a strategy, the part of fluency that transfers.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
In **Practice & Closure** — later in the lesson, a station, or homework — *not* in the opener. The opener’s job is to build strategy and discourse; this is where the volume reps live.

blocks.title: The both/and that resolves “but we need practice”

blocks.text: Don’t ask the opener to drill, and don’t drill in silence. Build the thinking in the opener (Number Talks, Same But Different), then do the reps here — with work shown and you circulating. Fluency needs both: understanding *and* practice. They just live in different parts of the lesson.
How to run it so it teaches

items: **Everyone shows work on paper** — the non-negotiable. No naked answers.
**You circulate** — this is the whole point. Watch *where* reasoning breaks, not just whether the answer is right.
**Respond in the moment** — a quick question or a brief why (“same-size pieces, so…”) right where the misconception is.
**Interleave the problem types** so students choose a strategy rather than repeat one.
**Debrief 2 minutes:** “What tripped people up?” Name the common error for the class.

blocks.text: Using a quiz tool (Quizizz, 99math, etc.) well

yes.title: Configure it like this
items: Self-paced, not the live speed race
Timer off or generous
Explanations turned on
Students still show work on paper as they go
You circulate while they work; always debrief

no.title: Avoid
items: Leaderboard speed competition as the main event
Treating the score as the outcome
Sitting at the desk watching the dashboard
No paper, no work, no debrief

blocks.text: The app delivers the problems; *you* still do the teaching by circulating, monitoring, and responding. The dashboard is a bonus, not the lesson.
Make the practice build fluency, not just speed

items: **Interleave:** mix a fraction, an integer, a percent, a ratio — so students decide which strategy applies (that’s flexibility).
**Space it (distributed practice):** short, frequent, revisiting earlier content — far more durable than one big block.
**Ask for the strategy,** not just the answer, on at least some items.

blocks.title: It connects back to the openers

blocks.text: The strategies students practice here are the ones surfaced in Number Talks and Number Strings. And yesterday’s practice or exit ticket becomes today’s *My Favorite No* — the misconceptions you spot while circulating are the best opener material you’ll find.

items: **Circulating + visible work** is how you reach a struggling student before a gap hardens — the opposite of finding out on a unit test.
**No speed pressure** protects the disposition of students who reason carefully.
**Include entry-friendly items** so every student gets reps they can succeed at, alongside the stretch ones.
